comparator.name: Dutch Language and Culture
comparator.sourceNotes: The current 2026–2027 Dutch-language programme has 60 EC in year one, 30 EC compulsory in year two, 50 EC of restricted choices across years two and three, 30 EC open electives and a 10 EC thesis. The Dutch Linguistics internal option follows the degree’s Dutch-language focus. Two compulsory and three first-listed eligible 10 EC choices are spread across the two spring terms. The formal regulations do not identify a graduation direction. They require prerequisites shown on the individual course records and board review where minor courses duplicate degree requirements. The year-one mentoring meetings and thesis seminar are required and carry no additional EC.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The first option responds directly through rhetoric, stylistics, language processing and mediated communication. The second responds through a sequence in literary interpretation, comparative cultural history and media. A third structural, historical and social linguistics option lacks enough substantive courses in language structure, change and variation to form a distinct coherent direction. Existing psycholinguistics, stylistics and beginner Dutch already contribute to the first option. Digital text corpora support the external degree without establishing a separate UCR data science direction.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both teach how arguments persuade and how to analyze them. UCR draws on classical and contemporary rhetorical practice.
Both examine how linguistic choices affect interpretation and persuasion. Leiden applies this to Dutch texts and discourse.
Both study persuasion in organized communication. UCR applies framing and persuasion to communication problems for local institutions.
Both examine how the mind processes language. Leiden also analyzes the structure and mental representation of Dutch.
Both introduce close reading and interpretation across literary genres. Leiden emphasizes Dutch literature.
Both compare theoretical approaches to literary interpretation. UCR applies them in a research project across literary traditions.
Leiden studies the role of digital tools and media in the humanities.
Leiden traces the history and development of Dutch.
Leiden studies Dutch literature and culture through 1800.
Leiden studies language use, meaning in context and indirect communication.
Leiden studies Dutch literature from 1800 onward.
Leiden trains students to interpret historical Dutch texts.
Leiden teaches academic writing and presenting in Dutch.
Leiden examines how media and genres influence language choices.
Leiden studies variation and the social dimensions of Dutch.
Leiden requires a core course in philosophy of science.
Leiden develops research methods for historical Dutch literature.
Leiden studies Dutch media in its social context.
Leiden continues its dedicated study of Dutch language structure and cognition.
Leiden examines rhetorical effects of Dutch word choices and grammatical constructions.
Leiden applies linguistics to multilingualism and language policy, including a project or short placement.
Leiden combines argument analysis with critical writing.
Leiden examines recent Dutch novels.
Leiden requires a 10 EC individual thesis and participation in the thesis seminar. UCR’s optional research sits outside the scheduled 180 EC.
Leiden sets aside 30 EC for open electives.

notes.text: Leiden develops specialist knowledge of Dutch language structure, variation and history alongside Dutch literature from the Middle Ages to the present. UCR covers related methods through rhetoric, language processing, literature and media. Its beginner Dutch course teaches everyday communication. Leiden also requires an individual thesis within the chosen subject area.

audience.programmeDescription: Leiden studies the Dutch language, older and modern Dutch literature, rhetoric, and how language and literature interact with media. Students apply these methods in a supervised thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: One UCR option focuses on language, persuasion and cognition. The other focuses on literature, cultural history and media. Both offer related academic methods. Leiden provides more depth in Dutch linguistics and Dutch literary history.
